name: Kolmogorov's Zero–One Law
statement: Any tail event of a sequence of independent random variables has probability exactly 0 or exactly 1, never anything in between.
meaning: A tail event is one whose occurrence does not depend on the outcome of any finite subset of the independent random variables; it is unaffected by changing finitely many of them. The law states such an event can only have probability 0 or 1, never an intermediate value. It thus splits tail events into those that almost surely happen and those that almost surely do not.
mechanism: The tail sigma-algebra is the intersection of the sigma-algebras generated by the variables from index n onward. By independence, any tail event is independent of each finite-dimensional sub-algebra and hence independent of the sigma-algebra they generate, which contains the tail event itself. An event independent of itself has probability equal to its square, forcing the probability to be 0 or 1.

examples.text: For a sequence of independent random variables, the event that the infinite sum converges is a tail event, so it happens with probability 0 or with probability 1.
For an i.i.d. coin-flip sequence, the event that a run of 100 consecutive heads occurs infinitely often is a tail event, hence has probability 0 or 1 (here, 1).
In percolation models the event that an infinite connected cluster exists is a tail-type event whose probability is 0 or 1, a fact used to justify critical-threshold arguments.

whyItMatters: It underlies why questions like whether a random walk returns to the origin infinitely often, or whether an infinite cluster exists, have deterministic yes/no answers rather than fractional probabilities. It is a foundational tool in probability theory, ergodic theory, and statistical physics.
limits: The law applies only to genuinely independent variables and only to tail events — it says nothing about events depending on finitely many coordinates, and it does not tell you which of the two values holds. Related but distinct results, such as the Hewitt–Savage zero-one law, apply to exchangeable rather than independent sequences.
misreadings: It does not say every event has probability 0 or 1, only tail events of independent variables, and it does not by itself reveal whether the answer is 0 or 1.
origin: Proved by Andrey Kolmogorov, appearing in his 1933 book "Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung," which axiomatised modern probability theory.
